newsitem.title: CANADA: Outlook seen bleak for Canadian heavy oil prices.
newsitem.headline: Outlook seen bleak for Canadian heavy oil prices.

text.p: The value of Canadian heavy oil is being driven down as an ever-growing torrent gushes into U.S. refining markets and analysts say the worst is yet to come on prices.

The price spread between Canadian light and heavy crudes has widened over the past two months to the highest level in 4-1/2 years amid billions of dollars worth of new development plans upstream but limited capacity to refine the thick oil.
The wide spreads come at a time when summer asphalt demand for paving and roofing projects usually lifts heavy oil and bitumen prices closer to light crude.

"We are very pessimistic on heavy oil differentials. Just too much capital is chasing this unlimited production upside, but there's a limited amount of refining capacity," said FirstEnergy Capital Corp analyst Martin Molyneaux.
"The refiners are going to take the boots to the producers, like the producers have done to them for three or four years now."

The spread between Edmonton par light sweet oil and Hardisty medium crude widened to C$6.50-C$7 (US$4.75-US$5.11) a barrel in May and June, about double the levels in the same period last year, according to new estimates from FirstEnergy.
So far, that has yet to convince heavy oil producers in Alberta and Saskatchewan, whose key export market is the U.S. Midwest, to cut back on plans to boost production.
The industry produced 530,000 barrels a day of heavy oil in the first quarter of 1997, up from 491,000 in the same period of 1996, figures from Purvin & Gertz show.

Production growth for bitumen, extra-heavy oil that must be expensively steamed to be produced from wells or mined, was even more dramatic, rising to 210,000 barrels a day in the first quarter from 150,000 in 1996.

A big part of the bitumen growth has come from Imperial Oil Ltd's expanding Cold Lake project in northeastern Alberta, which is expected to pump out an average of 115,000 barrels a day this year, up from about 90,000 last year.

Imperial has said it expected to increase Cold Lake production to 150,000 barrels a day by 2000 and several other producers, like Gulf Canada Resources Ltd, Shell Canada Ltd, Alberta Energy Co Ltd and Canadian Natural Resources Ltd, are at various stages of new heavy oil projects.
"The trend is pretty clear. I guess I'm not particularly surprised by the market," said Steve Kelly, oil markets analyst with Purvin & Gertz in Calgary.
Total Canadian crude oil production is pegged at just over two millon barrels a day.
Refiners' ability to process heavy oil has lagged far behind producers' ability to pump it out, analysts say.

"Pipelines and production are not the governing factors,. The governing factor is refining capacity. Hydrotreaters, hydrocreackers -- the whole works -- these are very expensive initiatives," Molyneaux said, adding that 80,000 barrels a day of new upgrading capacity cost about US$700 million.
Returns on invested capital among U.S. refiners, however, have averaged only a scant three-four percent over the past few years.
Also, the minimum time needed to take a processing addition at an existing refinery to completion is about 30 months and a "greenfield" project could take up to four years, Molyneaux said.
"It took us 14-15 months to dig ourselves out of putting out too much natural gas. This is going to take longer," he said. ((Reuters Calgary Bureau (403) 531-1624))
